speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me how long this painful ulcer on your leg has been present, and do you have a history of diabetes or peripheral vascular disease?

speaker: Patient
text: 54-year-old woman. The patient reports a skin lesion on her right leg that has been present for 1 month. The lesion began as a small red spot and has increased in size. She recalls an ant bite at the site before the lesion developed. She has a history of anterior uveitis treated with corticosteroids 8 months ago, as well as Crohn's disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your history of Crohn's disease and uveitis, I suspect this may be erythema nodosum or pyoderma gangrenosum, but I need to rule out infection. Have you experienced any systemic symptoms like fever, chills, or weight loss over the past month?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Painful ulcerative lesion on the right leg. I also have Lesion has a central necrotic base and purplish irregular borders, History of ant bite at the site of the lesion, Pitting pedal edema of the lower extremities, Dilated tortuous veins in both lower legs.

speaker: Doctor
text: The description of purplish irregular borders and central necrosis following minor trauma is highly suggestive of Pyoderma Gangrenosum, especially given your history of Crohn's disease. To confirm this diagnosis and rule out infection or vascular causes, I need to examine the wound directly. REQUEST IMAGES

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: ["Crohn's disease", 'Type 2 diabetes mellitus', 'Hypertension', 'Treated for anterior uveitis 8 months ago'] Social history: Recently returned from a visit to Wisconsin 2 months ago.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that information. Given your recent travel to Wisconsin, I need to rule out Sporotrichosis, a fungal infection often acquired from soil or plant matter. Have you had any exposure to thorny plants, soil, or cats while in Wisconsin?

speaker: Doctor
text: The history of Crohn's disease, anterior uveitis, and the characteristic purplish, necrotic ulcer following minor trauma (pathergy) strongly points to Pyoderma Gangrenosum rather than an infectious cause. I will now request a biopsy of the lesion edge to confirm the diagnosis and rule out malignancy or infection. REQUEST TEST: Skin_Biopsy
